tooley.q: A multifunction display (MFD) can be:
opts: set to display information from the standby magnetic compass
configured for more than one type of information
used only for basic flight information
tooley.explain: An MFD is a configurable display: weather radar, navigation map, checklists, or a substitute for the PFD/ND if either fails (Tooley 1.1.5.6).

tooley.q: Which standby instruments are driven from the aircraft's pitot-static system:
opts: Airspeed indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator
Airspeed indicator, altimeter and angle-of-attack indicator
Airspeed indicator, vertical speed indicator and magnetic compass
tooley.explain: The three air data instruments (ASI, altimeter, VSI) use static and pitot pressure. The magnetic compass is an independent magnetic device and needs no pitot-static supply.

tooley.q: Static pressure is fed:
opts: only to the airspeed indicator and vertical speed indicator
to the airspeed indicator as well as the altimeter and vertical speed indicator
tooley.explain: Static pressure goes to all three instruments; only the ASI additionally receives ram (pitot) pressure to compare against (Figure 1.11).

tooley.q: The horizontal situation indicator (HSI) uses information derived from:
tooley.explain: The HSI combines compass and radio navigation (VOR) information to show the horizontal situation (Tooley Table 1.1).

tooley.q: The term 'glass cockpit' refers to:
opts: the use of LCD and CRT displays
the use of toughened glass windows
the use of a transparent partition between the flight deck and passenger cabin
tooley.explain: A "glass cockpit" uses CRT and LCD screens in place of electromechanical dials (Tooley section 1.1).

tooley.q: Basic air data instruments are:
opts: airspeed indicator, vertical speed indicator and artificial horizon
airspeed indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass
airspeed indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator
tooley.explain: The three pitot-static driven instruments are called air data instruments: ASI, altimeter, VSI.

tooley.q: Three airborne parameters that can be used to assess aircraft position are:
tooley.explain: Heading, airspeed and height are the basic quantities that fix the aircraft's position; weight is not a position parameter.

tooley.q: The instrument shown in Figure 1.27 is the:
tooley.explain: The dial is marked "IAS KNOTS" with a 60 to 400 scale: it is an airspeed indicator (ASI).

tooley.q: Engine parameters such as turbine speed are displayed on:
tooley.explain: ECAM (Airbus) and EICAS (Boeing) show engine parameters; the EADI and EHSI are flight and navigation displays.

tooley.q: The aircraft slip indicator is found in the:
tooley.explain: The EADI contains the slip indicator (together with the attitude display, command bars, glide slope pointer, localiser indicator).

tooley.q: Where is the 'rising runway':
tooley.explain: The symbolic runway (rising runway) is the localiser indicator on the EADI; it appears once the pilot has acquired the glide slope.

tooley.q: Under visual flight rules (VFR) the pilot's most important source of information concerning the aircraft's position and attitude is:
opts: the altimeter and vertical speed indicators
the view out of the cockpit window
the airspeed indicator and the magnetic compass
tooley.explain: Tooley section 1.1: under VFR the most important source of information is the view out of the cockpit window.

tooley.q: The EFIS fitted to a large aircraft usually consists of:
opts: separate primary flight and navigation displays
a primary display with several standby instruments
tooley.explain: The EFIS consists of a PFD (or EADI) and an ND (or EHSI), duplicated for the captain and first officer (Tooley 1.1.5).

tooley.q: The instrument shown in Figure 1.28 is the:
tooley.explain: The figure shows "HDG", VOR, WPT, distance and a rotating compass: it is the EHSI (horizontal situation).

tooley.q: The instrument shown in Figure 1.29 is the:
tooley.explain: The figure has the attitude horizon (±10, ±20 pitch scale), command bars, glide slope, LAND 3 and VNAV modes: it is the EADI.

tooley.q: In a basic 'T' configuration of instruments:
opts: the ASI appears on the left and the altimeter appears on the right
the ADI appears on the left and the ASI appears on the right
the ADI appears on the left and the HSI appears on the right
tooley.explain: The T: ASI left, ADI top centre, altimeter right, HSI below the ADI (Tooley Figure 1.23).

tooley.q: The flight director system receives information:
opts: only from the attitude gyro and altimeter
tooley.explain: The flight director takes data from the attitude gyro, the VOR/localiser/glide slope receiver, the radar altimeter, the compass system and barometric sensors (Tooley 1.1.4).

tooley.q: EICAS provides the following information:
tooley.explain: EICAS shows engine parameters, crew alerts and system pages (electrical, hydraulic, fuel...); navigation data belongs to the ND.

tooley.q: The two sets of flight regulations that a pilot may fly by are:
tooley.explain: VFR (visual flight rules) and IFR (instrument flight rules).

tooley.q: A major advantage of EFIS is a reduction in:
opts: moving parts present in the flight deck
tooley.explain: EFIS replaces electromechanical dials with static screens, cutting moving parts. EFIS actually increases EMI (Tooley section 15.2), it does not reduce it.

tooley.q: The term 'artificial horizon' is sometimes used to describe the indication produced by:
tooley.explain: The attitude indicator shows the aircraft relative to the horizon, hence the name artificial horizon (Tooley Table 1.1).

tooley.q: Typical displays on an EHSI are:
tooley.explain: The EHSI shows heading, track, VOR/DME/ILS/ADF, wind and range (Tooley 1.1.3.2). Altitude and vertical speed belong to the PFD.

tooley.q: In a basic 'T' configuration of instruments:
opts: the ADI appears at the top and the HSI appears at the bottom
the HSI appears at the top and the ASI appears at the bottom
the ASI appears at the top and the ADI appears at the bottom
tooley.explain: The top bar of the T holds ASI, ADI, altimeter; the ADI is top centre and the HSI sits directly below it.

tooley.q: Operational faults in FMS can be detected by:
opts: routine maintenance inspection of the aircraft
automatically comparing outputs on a continuous basis
tooley.explain: The two FMSs (captain and first officer) compare indications and outputs continuously to detect faults (Tooley 1.1.8).

tooley.q: The display marked X in Figure 1.30 is the:
tooley.explain: X points at the unit on the centre pedestal between the two pilot seats: the FMS CDU.

tooley.q: The display marked Y in Figure 1.31 is the:
tooley.explain: Y points at the large screen directly in front of the captain: the primary flight display (PFD).

tooley.q: The upper ECAM display provides:
tooley.explain: The upper ECAM screen (E/WD) shows engine parameters and warnings; the lower one shows system pages (Tooley 1.1.6).

tooley.q: The peak wavelength of light emitted from a red LED is typically:
tooley.explain: Tooley Table 11.1 gives 635 nm for red LEDs (the miniature type 690 nm). 475 nm is blue, 525 nm is green.

tooley.q: The spectral response of the human eye peaks at around:
tooley.explain: The eye is most sensitive near 550 nm (green light), Figure 11.12; the lecture gives a 555 nm peak.

tooley.q: Adjacent phosphors of blue and green are illuminated on the screen of a CRT. The resultant colour produced will be:
tooley.explain: Green + blue = cyan; red + green = yellow; red + blue = magenta; all three = white (Figure 11.9).

tooley.q: The human eye is most sensitive to:
tooley.explain: The correct answer is green (peak near 550 nm, consistent with question 2, Figure 11.12 and lecture slide 6). Note: the answer key printed in Tooley (Appendix 3, A.11) gives question 4 as (a), which contradicts the chapter's own question 2, so it is treated as a printing error; the site uses (c).
tooley.src: Tooley Ch.11 Q4 (printed key says (a), site uses (c): see explanation)

tooley.q: A seven-segment LED display has segments a, b, c, d and g illuminated. The character displayed will be:
tooley.explain: Segments a, b, c, d, g form a 3. A 2 needs e instead of c; a 5 needs f instead of b. (Checked in the notebook.)

tooley.q: The BCD input to a seven-segment display decoder is 1001. The digit displayed will be:
tooley.explain: 1001₂ = 9 (BCD). The digit 8 has code 1000.

tooley.q: The potential at the grid of a CRT is:
opts: negative with respect to the cathode
positive with respect to the cathode
tooley.explain: The grid is held negative with respect to the cathode to repel electrons, which controls brightness (Tooley 11.1.1).

tooley.q: The function of the final anode of a CRT is:
opts: controlling the brightness of the display
tooley.explain: The final anode sits at a very high positive potential (several kilovolts) to accelerate the beam; deflection is by X/Y plates or coils, brightness by the grid.

tooley.q: Electromagnetic deflection of a CRT uses:
opts: X- and Y-plates inside the CRT
coils around the neck of the CRT
tooley.explain: Electromagnetic deflection uses two sets of coils placed externally around the neck of the tube; X and Y plates inside are electrostatic deflection.

tooley.q: The three beams in a colour CRT are associated with the colours:
tooley.explain: The three electron guns correspond to the red, green and blue phosphors (RGB).

tooley.q: When compared with CRT displays, AMLCD displays have:
tooley.explain: The main AMLCD advantages are weight, power, volume and reliability (Tooley, chapter 11 introduction).

tooley.q: The final anode of a CRT display requires:
tooley.explain: The final anode needs a steady high positive potential (several kilovolts DC) to accelerate the beam.

tooley.q: The deflecting waveform supplied to the plates of an electrostatic CRT will be:
tooley.explain: Raster scanning uses ramp (sawtooth) waveforms at two different frequencies on the X and Y plates.

tooley.q: The typical value of maximum forward current for an LED indicator is:
tooley.explain: Table 11.1: maximum forward current is 30 to 40 mA, i.e. 0.03 to 0.04 A.

tooley.q: The patterns required to display alphanumeric characters in a CRT controller are stored in:
tooley.explain: Character shapes are fixed, so they live in a character generator ROM (Figure 11.11).

tooley.q: When compared with passive matrix LCDs, AMLCDs are:
tooley.explain: Passive matrices respond slowly and are less sharp; the AMLCD uses a TFT per cell, so it is faster and sharper (Tooley 11.3.2, 11.3.3).

tooley.q: The standard for ACARS is defined in:
tooley.explain: ACARS was originally specified in ARINC 597 and revised as ARINC 724B (Tooley 15.1).

tooley.q: Engine parameters are displayed on:
tooley.explain: ECAM (Airbus) shows engine and system parameters; the EHSI is a navigation display and the CDU is the FMS data entry unit.

tooley.q: The left and right cockpit displays:
opts: are supplied from separate symbol generators at all times
will only be supplied from the same symbol generator when all other symbol generators have failed
are supplied from the same symbol generator
tooley.explain: The left generator feeds the captain's displays, the right one the first officer's, the centre one is a backup; only when the others have failed do both sides share one generator (Tooley 15.2.2).

tooley.q: On a flight deck EFIS system, if all of the displays were missing information from a particular source, the most likely cause would be:
opts: the display controller and symbol generator
the sensor, input bus or display controller
tooley.explain: A fault common to every display lies upstream of all of them: the source sensor, the input bus or the display controller; not one individual symbol generator.

tooley.q: A central maintenance computer provides:
opts: ground and BITE testing using a portable control panel
ground and in-flight monitoring and testing
display of system warnings and cautions
tooley.explain: The CMC collects fault and status data from the LRUs continuously, in flight and on the ground; displaying warnings is the job of the FWC/ECAM.

tooley.q: The sweep voltage waveform used on an electromagnetic CRT is:
tooley.explain: Because the deflection coils have resistance, the scan voltage must be trapezoidal rather than the straight sawtooth of an electrostatic CRT (Tooley 15.2.2).

tooley.q: In an EFIS with three symbol generators, what is the purpose of the third symbol generator?
opts: comparison with the pilot's symbol generator
tooley.explain: The centre generator is a backup that can replace the left or right one on failure (Tooley 15.2.2).

tooley.q: The ACARS system uses channels in the:
tooley.explain: ACARS uses the VHF band 129 to 137 MHz (Tooley 15.1, Table 15.1).

tooley.q: If one EICAS CRT fails:
opts: the standby CRT will automatically take over
the remaining CRT will display primary EICAS data
the FMS CDU will display the failed CRT data
tooley.explain: The remaining screen displays the primary EICAS data; secondary pages are called up from the control panel when needed.

tooley.q: A method used in modern aircraft for reporting in-flight faults to an engineering and monitoring ground station is:
tooley.explain: ACARS sends performance, fault and maintenance data from the aircraft to the airline over the VHF link.

floyd.q: Would you select a decoder/driver with active-HIGH or active-LOW outputs to drive a common-cathode 7-segment LED display?
floyd.explain: A common-cathode display lights a segment when its anode is driven HIGH, so active-HIGH outputs are needed. The 74HC47 has active-LOW outputs, so it suits common-anode displays (Floyd p.339).
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6 · Section 6–5 Checkup #3 (p.341; answer p.384)

floyd.q: In the 7-segment display multiplexing system of Figure 6-49, which IC enables the two displays alternately?
floyd.explain: The 74HC139 (a decoder) enables digit A and digit B in turn; the 74HC157 selects the BCD code; the 74HC47 decodes to 7 segments.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6 · Section 6–8 Checkup #4(c) (p.356; answer p.384)

floyd.q: In the same system (Figure 6-49), what does the 74HC157 do?
opts: Decodes the BCD to energise the display
Multiplexes the two BCD codes to the 7-segment decoder
floyd.explain: The 74HC157 is a 4-bit data selector (multiplexer): the select line LOW passes the LSD code, HIGH passes the MSD code.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6 · Section 6–8 Checkup #4(a) (p.356; answer p.384)

floyd.q: With the 74HC47, when the LT (lamp test) input is LOW and BI/RBO is HIGH:
floyd.explain: Lamp test turns on all seven segments to verify that none is burned out (Floyd p.339).

floyd.q: Why does the 7-segment display use lowercase b and d instead of capital B and D?
opts: A capital B would look like an 8 and a capital D like a 0
Capital letters do not exist in hexadecimal
floyd.explain: Floyd p.244: the letter b is lowercase because a capital B would be the same as the digit 8; similarly a capital D would look like 0.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.4 · Applied Logic: Seven-Segment Display (p.244)

floyd.q: Which statement correctly compares LED and LCD 7-segment displays?
opts: An LCD can be seen in the dark, an LED cannot
Both emit light on their own
An LED can be seen in the dark, an LCD cannot
floyd.explain: Each LED segment is a light-emitting diode, so it makes its own light. An LCD works by polarising light; an activated segment does not reflect light and appears black, so it cannot be seen in the dark (Floyd p.244).
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.4 · Applied Logic: Seven-Segment Display (p.244)

floyd.q: According to Floyd Table 4-14, which segments form the letter C?
floyd.explain: Table 4-14: C = a, d, e, f. (b: c,d,e,f,g; d: b,c,d,e,g; E: a,d,e,f,g; A: a,b,c,e,f,g.)

generated.q: With a visual acuity of 1 arcminute (2.91×10⁻⁴ rad), the smallest size the eye can still resolve at 10 m is:
generated.explain: h = D·θ = 10 m × 2.91×10⁻⁴ = 2.91×10⁻³ m = 2.91 mm (matches the lecture table).

generated.q: How many times more pixels does a 4K UHD screen (3840×2160) have than Full HD (1920×1080)?
generated.explain: Twice the width and twice the height gives 2×2 = 4 times as many pixels (8,294,400 versus 2,073,600).

generated.q: A CRT scans 400 lines with a vertical scan frequency of 100 Hz. The horizontal sawtooth frequency needed is:
generated.explain: f_X = N_lines × f_Y = 400 × 100 Hz = 40,000 Hz = 40 kHz (Tooley example in section 11.1.3).

generated.q: A standard 5 mm LED at 10 mA with 2.0 V forward drop on a 5 V supply needs a series resistor of (the module's own worked example):
If each R, G, B channel has 256 levels, how many colours can one pixel represent?
generated.explain: 256 × 256 × 256 = 256³ = 16,777,216, matching "more than 16 million colours" in Tooley 11.3.3.

generated.q: On the Airbus A320, which computer generates the images and symbols for the PFD, ND and ECAM?
generated.explain: The DMC generates the display information; the FWC generates warnings; the SDAC collects system data and passes it to the DMCs.

generated.q: According to Tooley (section 1.1.6), N2 on the ECAM display is:
generated.explain: Tooley: "N1/fan speed, EGT, N2/high pressure turbine speed". The lecture's E/WD slide calling N2 low pressure is wrong.

generated.q: According to the lecture, which liquid crystal alignment technology leads in modern aircraft displays?
generated.explain: Slide 4: TN was used in early aircraft displays (now less common), IPS is "widely used in modern aircraft displays (leader)", MVA is used in high-end cockpits.

generated.q: ECAM FUEL page with the pumps off: tanks of 686, 2742, 5852, 2741 and 686 kg. The fuel on board (FOB) is:
generated.explain: 686 + 2742 + 5852 + 2741 + 686 = 12,707 kg, exactly the FOB value on the slide.

generated.q: In ACARS, which four events does an OOOI message report?
opts: out of the gate, off the ground, on the ground, into the gate
generated.explain: OOOI = Out, Off, On, In (lecture slide 20).

generated.q: The ND slide shows 37 NM to a waypoint at a ground speed of 257 kt. The estimated flight time is about:
generated.explain: t = 37 NM / 257 kt = 0.144 h ≈ 8.6 minutes. So the label "23 33" as a time of 23 min 33 s is doubtful (it may be a UTC clock time).

generated.q: The A320 (1988) introduced the "full display" cockpit with how many main CRT screens?
generated.explain: Two PFDs, two NDs and two ECAM screens = 6 (slides 8 and 11).

generated.q: On the PFD attitude indicator, the upper half (sky) and lower half (ground) are coloured:
generated.explain: The standard artificial horizon convention: blue sky above, brown ground below (slide 21).

generated.q: At FL140 in the ISA standard atmosphere with a cabin altitude of 2,870 ft, the cabin differential pressure ΔP is closest to:
generated.explain: p(2,870 ft) ≈ 13.23 psi, p(14,000 ft) ≈ 8.63 psi, so ΔP ≈ 4.6 psi. The slide shows 2.9 psi, so it is only an illustrative number.

generated.q: Which standard governs the quality of airborne electronic HARDWARE?
generated.explain: DO-160: environment; DO-178: software; DO-254: hardware (slide 2).
